title: Memory layout and speed
objectives: See how contiguous memory speeds up a loop.

screens.title: Fetched in rows of eight
screens.prose: A `std::vector<double>` of 24 prices sits in one unbroken block of memory. The processor never fetches a single double from memory: it fetches the 64 bytes around it, 8 doubles, drawn here as one row.

state.caption: Each row of 8 doubles is 64 bytes, fetched together.

screens.question: A loop reads `x[0]`, `x[1]`, ..., `x[23]` in order. How many fetches from memory does it make?

hints.text: After `x[0]` arrives, where are `x[1]` to `x[7]`?
The first row arrives in one fetch.
24 doubles, 8 per fetch.

feedback.correct: Three fetches: the other 21 reads were already there.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count rows, not numbers.

byKey.each: You counted one fetch per double. The fetch for `x[0]` brings `x[1]` to `x[7]` with it.
byKey.bytes: 192 is the number of bytes. The question counts fetches of 64 bytes each.

explain.text: The 64-byte block is a **cache line**. Reading in order uses all 8 doubles of each line before the next fetch: **sequential access**. That is why a loop over a vector is fast.

screens.title: Jumping eight at a time
screens.prose: Now a loop with a **stride** of 8: it reads `x[0]`, `x[8]`, `x[16]`, then comes back for `x[1]`, `x[9]`, `x[17]`, and so on. Same 24 reads, different order.

state.caption: Tap to mark the cells the loop reads.

screens.question: Tap the three cells the stride-8 loop reads first.

hints.text: Start at `x[0]` and add 8 each time.
The first read.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at index 0 and jump by 8.

byKey.c1: `x[1]` comes fourth, after the loop has visited all three rows once.
byKey.c7: Index 7 is the end of the first line, not a step of 8 from 0.

explain.text: Every read lands on a new line, so each fetch delivers one useful double out of eight. In a big array the loop returns for `x[1]` long after its line was pushed out, and fetches it again.

canvas.caption: Stride 8: a new line for every read.

screens.title: A matrix in one line
screens.prose: A matrix is stored the same way: row 0, then row 1, and so on. The number in each cell is its place in memory. Summing **row by row** walks memory in order; **column by column** jumps a whole row each step.

state.caption: Blue: row by row. Green: column by column.

screens.question: A 1,000 by 1,000 matrix of doubles. Suppose no cache line survives until a walk comes back to it. How many line fetches does the row-by-row sum make?

hints.text: Row by row reads memory in order, like the 24 prices.
How many doubles are there, and how many share a line?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count doubles, then divide by 8 per line.

byKey.col: A million fetches is the column-by-column walk: one line per read. Row by row uses all 8 doubles of each line.
byKey.rows: 1,000 is the number of rows. Each row of 1,000 doubles spans 125 lines.

explain.text: Row by row: $10^6 / 8 = 125{,}000$ fetches. Column by column: each step jumps 1,000 doubles, so up to $10^6$ fetches, eight times as many. Real caches keep some lines, so the gap is smaller, but it stays large.

screens.title: Row and column to place
screens.prose: Row `i` starts after `i` full rows of `cols` numbers. Then step `j` along it. Write the index function every flat matrix needs.
screens.question: Write `index(i, j, cols)`: the place of row `i`, column `j` in a row-major matrix with `cols` columns.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Six hidden tests, including a matrix of one row and a row of exactly 8 doubles.

hints.text: How many numbers come before row `i`?
Row 2 starts at place 16 = 2 × 8.
`return i * cols + j;`

feedback.correct: `i * cols + j`: skip `i` rows, then `j` places.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Row 2, column 3 with 8 columns should be 19. If you got 26, you multiplied `j` by `cols` instead of `i`: rows and columns swapped.
byKey.test-3: Row 2, column 3 of a 4-column matrix is 11. Check which index is multiplied by `cols`.

explain.text: Row `i` begins at `i * cols`; column `j` is `j` places further. Swapping to `j * cols + i` still compiles and still stays in range for a square matrix, which is why that bug hides.

screens.title: Two walks, one sum
screens.prose: Write both walks over the same flat matrix. They add the same numbers in a different order, so the tests only check the sums. Speed is the next screen's question.
screens.question: Write `sum_row_major` and `sum_col_major`. Both read `m[i * cols + j]`; only the loop order differs.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Seven hidden tests: 2 × 3 and 3 × 2 matrices, a single row, a 2 × 8 matrix and a million entries. The library's index check stops any read past the end.

hints.text: Both functions use the same index, `i * cols + j`.
Row major: `for i` outside, `for j` inside. Column major: the other way round.
Swapping only the loops, never the index, keeps both sums right.

feedback.correct: Same index, same sum, different order in memory.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: The 2 × 3 sum is wrong. Did you write `i * rows + j`? A row is `cols` long, so row `i` starts at `i * cols`.
byKey.test-2: Column major should still read `m[i * cols + j]`; only the loops swap.
byKey.test-3: The 3 × 2 sum is wrong. Check the index uses `cols`, not `rows`.

explain.text: Both functions add every entry once, so the sums match. Row major reads places 0, 1, 2, ...; column major reads 0, `cols`, `2 * cols`, ...: a stride of a whole row.

screens.title: Predict, then read the desk's run
screens.prose: A desk times your two functions on a 2,000 by 2,000 matrix: 4 million doubles, 32 MB. Built with `g++ -O2`, median of 7 runs. Predict before you see the times.
screens.question: Which walk is faster, and by roughly how much?

options.text: Row by row, several times faster
Row by row, but only a few per cent faster
options.why: You expected a small gap. Column by column fetches up to eight times as many lines, and memory is far slower than arithmetic.

options.text: The same: both do 4 million additions
options.why: The additions are the same; the fetches are not. Time here is spent waiting for memory, not adding.
Column by column jumps 2,000 doubles (16 KB) each step, so almost every read needs a new line.

hints.text: Which walk uses all 8 doubles of each line it fetches?
Row by row reads memory in order; column by column jumps 16 KB each step.

feedback.correct: Row by row, about seven times faster on the desk's machine.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cache lines each walk fetches.

byKey.same: You counted additions. The time goes on fetching lines: one per 8 reads row by row, nearly one per read column by column.

explain.text: On the desk machine, row by row took 2.9 ms and column by column 21.5 ms: about 7 times slower, for the same sum. In order, the processor also fetches the next lines before they are asked for.

screens.title: The whole lattice, flat
screens.prose: Level 2 kept one row of the tree. Now keep every node, in one flat vector: node $(i, j)$, after $i$ steps with $j$ ups, at index $i(n + 1) + j$. Here $n = 3$: the number in each cell is its index.
screens.question: Write `flat_lattice_price`: the same European call as level 2, stored on the flat lattice.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Six hidden tests: $n$ = 1, 4, 128 and 512 (within 0.005 of Black-Scholes, £10.4506), and a strike of £110. Prices are accepted within a relative 1e-9.

hints.text: Leaves first: `v[n * w + j]` is the payoff at $S u^j d^{n-j}$.
Node $(i, j)$ reads its children at $(i + 1, j + 1)$ and $(i + 1, j)$.

feedback.correct: The same price as level 2: £10.4467 at $n = 512$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: At $n = 4$ the price should be 9.9705. Check the leaves go in row `n` and that each node reads row `i + 1`.
byKey.test-4: At $n = 512$ the price should be 10.4467. A crash here usually means an index past the end: the last row is `n`, not `n + 1`.

explain.text: It works, but it is wasteful on purpose: at $n = 512$ the lattice holds $513^2$ doubles, 2.1 MB, and nearly half are never used. Level 2's one row is 513 doubles, 4 KB, which stays in the fastest cache. Keep the whole lattice only when you need every node, for Greeks or exercise boundaries.

screens.title: Rows in different places
screens.prose: The C++ course built a lattice as `std::vector<std::vector<double>>`. A colleague wants it for the pricer's hot loop: "a vector is contiguous, so a vector of vectors is one block". Each box below is one heap block.
screens.question: Is `v[1][0]` stored right after `v[0][2]` in memory?

options.text: No: each row is its own heap block, wherever the allocator put it
Yes: a vector is contiguous, so the rows follow one another
options.why: The outer vector is contiguous, but it holds three small row objects, each pointing to its own block. The numbers are not in the outer vector.

options.text: Yes, as long as every row has the same length
options.why: Equal lengths do not make one block. Each inner vector still allocates separately.

options.text: Yes, once you call `reserve` on the outer vector
options.why: `reserve` sizes the outer vector's own block of row objects. Each row's numbers still live in a separate allocation.

hints.text: What does the outer vector hold: numbers, or row objects?
Follow an arrow from the outer vector.
Each inner vector makes its own allocation.

feedback.correct: Every row is a separate block: one more pointer to follow and no guarantee of order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the outer vector holds.

byKey.yes: You applied "contiguous" to the numbers. The outer vector is contiguous, but it holds row objects that point to separate blocks.

explain.text: A vector of vectors costs an extra pointer jump per row and scatters the rows across the heap. For a hot loop use one flat `std::vector<double>` with `i * cols + j`, as you just did. NumPy arrays and pandas columns are flat blocks for the same reason.

screens.title: Arrays of structs, structs of arrays
screens.prose:
The rule behind every screen: a loop pays for the lines it touches, not the numbers it uses.

```cpp
struct Tick { double price; double size; long long time; };  // 24 bytes
std::vector<Tick> ticks;              // array of structs: p s t p s t
std::vector<double> prices, sizes;    // struct of arrays: p p p p
```

$$\text{lines} \approx \frac{N \times \text{bytes from one value to the next}}{64}$$

state.caption: Array of structs: prices (highlighted) share their lines with sizes and times.

screens.question: A loop sums the prices of 100,000 ticks stored as `std::vector<Tick>`. How many cache lines does it read?

hints.text: From one price to the next is a whole `Tick`: 24 bytes.

feedback.correct: 37,500 lines; stored as a separate `prices` vector it would be 12,500.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply 100,000 by the 24 bytes between prices, then divide by 64.

byKey.soa: 12,500 is the struct-of-arrays count, prices packed 8 to a line. Here each price drags its size and time along.
byKey.each: That is one line per tick. Two or three ticks share each 64-byte line.

explain.text: $100{,}000 \times 24 / 64 = 37{,}500$ lines, three times the 12,500 of a separate price column. A loop that needs only prices wants a **struct of arrays**; code that handles whole ticks one at a time is happy with an **array of structs**.

screens.title: A buffer of ticks
screens.prose: A strategy keeps the last 100,000 tick prices, appends new ticks at the end and scans the whole buffer every second. A desk run compares two containers: `g++ -O2`, one scan, median of 21 runs.
screens.question: Which container should hold the buffer?

options.why: True, but the buffer is scanned every second. Each list node is its own heap block with two pointers, so the scan chases pointers instead of reading lines in order.
A map is a tree of separate nodes too, and the ticks already arrive in time order. Sorted inserts buy nothing here.
Each inner vector is a separate block, so the scan jumps between blocks. One flat vector is simpler and faster.

hints.text: Which operation happens most: appending, or scanning?
Read the two scan times.
The scan wants contiguous memory; `reserve` stops the appends from reallocating.

feedback.correct: A flat, reserved vector: contiguous scans and no reallocation.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The buffer is scanned every second.

byKey.list: You chose the list for cheap appends, but the scan dominates and the list scans about three times slower, more as nodes scatter.

explain.text: The list's nodes were allocated in order in this test, so it was only three times slower; in a long-running process they scatter and the gap grows. pandas and NumPy store each column as one flat block for this reason. An order book (the C++ course's maps lesson) is often a flat array indexed by price tick for the same reason.

ideas: Memory arrives in 64-byte cache lines of 8 doubles, so reading in order uses every double fetched.
Store a matrix or lattice in one flat `std::vector<double>` at `i * cols + j`, and loop with the last index innermost.
Lists, maps and vectors of vectors scatter their data across the heap; a reserved flat vector, or a struct of arrays, keeps a hot loop on contiguous memory.
summary.trap: A `std::vector<std::vector<double>>` is not one block: each row is a separate allocation.

quiz.prose: A matrix of 1 row and 1,000 columns, stored row by row.
quiz.question: Which sum is faster: row by row, or column by column?

options.text: Neither: both read places 0, 1, ..., 999 in order
Row by row, about 8 times faster
options.why: With one row, the column walk steps from column 0 to column 1 to column 2: the same addresses in the same order.
Each column has one entry, so the column walk is the same walk through memory.

feedback.correct: One row: both walks are the same walk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out the first three indices each walk reads.

explain.text: With `rows = 1`, `i` is always 0 and the index is just `j`. Both orders read 0, 1, 2, ..., so they cost the same. The gap appears only when a column step jumps a whole row.

quiz.prose: You `push_back` 100,000 prices into an empty `std::vector<double>` without `reserve`. Its capacity doubles when full: 1, 2, 4, ..., 131,072. Each growth copies every element into the new block.
quiz.question: About how many element copies do all the growths make in total?

feedback.correct: About 131,000 copies, plus 17 new blocks. `reserve(100000)` makes it zero copies and one block.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the sizes of the full blocks that are copied.

byKey.growths: 17 is how many times it grows. The question asks how many elements are copied in all.
byKey.n: 100,000 is the number of appends. Each growth copies the whole block so far: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... .

explain.text: The block is copied when full at sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., 65,536: $2^{17} - 1 = 131{,}071$ copies. That is less than two per element on average, but each growth also allocates and frees a block. `reserve` removes all of it.

quiz.prose: A flat lattice for $n = 512$ stores node $(i, j)$ at `v[i * (n + 1) + j]`.
quiz.question: At which index is node $(3, 2)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each row holds $n + 1 = 513$ places.

byKey.n: You used rows of 512. A lattice row holds $n + 1 = 513$ nodes.

explain.text: Row 3 starts after 3 rows of 513 places, at 1,539; node $j = 2$ is two further, at 1,541.

quiz.prose: A 1,000 by 8 matrix of doubles, stored row by row, each row starting on a cache-line boundary. Assume no line survives until a walk returns to it.
quiz.question: How many line fetches does the row-by-row sum make?

widget.accept: 1,000: each row of 8 doubles is exactly one line.

feedback.correct: One line per row, 1,000 in all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many bytes is one row?

byKey.col: 8,000 is the column-by-column count, when no line survives. Row by row reads each line once.
byKey.eight: You divided rows by 8. Each row is already 64 bytes: a whole line.

explain.text: A row is 8 × 8 = 64 bytes, one line exactly, so row by row fetches 1,000 lines. The column walk revisits each line 8 times; if lines did not survive, it would fetch 8,000.
